cases.title: Tbilisi–Rustavi road, Ponichala: 435 properties bought out, 57 red-list trees cut
cases.place: Ponichala, Tbilisi, and the Tbilisi–Rustavi highway section, Georgia
cases.point: Ponichala, on the Tbilisi–Rustavi highway alignment, where the complainant buildings 12 v/g, 16 a/b and 28a stand (approximate; the ADB reports do not give coordinates)

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Loan 3063-GEO for Tranche 3 of the Sustainable Urban Transport Investment Program. ADB provided $73 million of a $118.2 million total project cost. The project was classed A for involuntary resettlement and B for environment, but was monitored as if it were category A for environment. The revised project closure date on ADB's website was 18 July 2020 (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Second Annual Monitoring Report, 11 November 2019).

cases.conditions: The loan financed a section of the Tbilisi–Rustavi road. At the borrower's request the road scope was cut from 6.8 km to 3.5 km. Land acquisition and resettlement plans (LARP 2a and 2b) governed the buy-outs, and ADB's Compliance Review Panel imposed a remedial action plan after finding the project non-compliant in six areas, including noise, vibration and vulnerable groups; the remedial measures were disclosed in April and May 2018 (ADB semi-annual social monitoring report, January–June 2018; ADB CRP, Second Annual Monitoring Report, 2019).
cases.community: ADB's own monitoring records what was taken. Under LARP 2a, covering Section 2 Part A, 243 of 244 privately owned properties had been acquired as of the end of June 2018; the only one left was the GMP Pharmaceutical Company. Under LARP 2b, covering Section 2 Part B, all 192 properties were acquired, which the report breaks down as all 151 privately owned properties and all 41 apartments. A structural integrity study carried out in 2015 by Nord Est Progetti Srl of Italy recommended dismantling a two-storey residential building with 41 apartments; the same study concluded that construction would not cause a risk of collapse or damage to nine other multi-apartment buildings. An application dated 11 January 2018 came from residents of building #8 on Rustavi Highway asking for a state-owned two-storey building to be dismantled and the debris removed; the Municipal Development Fund did so. One claimant whose property had been transferred to state ownership through expropriation 'left the building on own accord, as a result of negotiations'. Compensation was paid into bank accounts; the report gives no amounts and no relocation counts (ADB semi-annual social monitoring report, January–June 2018). For the project as a whole the Compliance Review Panel writes that construction of Section 2, 6.8 km, 'will involve' acquisition of 312 land plots with 29.5 hectares of land and demolition of 692 structures (82 residential, 90 industrial and commercial, 520 minor), and that 282 households and 33 businesses 'will be affected' — planned figures, not a count of what had happened. The Panel also records that it 'was also informed that 57 trees falling within the national red list ... have already been cut and removed from the National Forest Park due to construction of the road', with replanting not yet done by November 2019 though the fund had reportedly paid money compensation for the cutting in advance. A construction material dump that the Municipal Development Fund estimated at about 160,000 cubic metres sat next to both the residential areas of Ponichala and the industrial area. A 60-metre retaining wall foundation sits in the Mtkvari riverbed, three 20-metre sections of it built in July and August 2019 when the water was low; the main body could not be concreted because works stopped, so long sections of reinforcement bars protrude from the river (ADB CRP, Second Annual Monitoring Report, 11 November 2019). Residents of three Ponichala apartment blocks complained to ADB about noise and vibration: 81 residents of building 12 v/g on 14 March 2016, 72 residents of building 16 a/b on 10 November 2016, and 30 residents of building 28a on 21 June 2018. The Panel's wording for building 28a is that strong evidence of noncompliance, the lack of assessment of vibration impact, 'was linked to likely harm to the third group of complainants'. Its 2019 report records no confirmed physical damage to the complainants' buildings and says that 'no construction activity had occurred in the areas where the complainants reside during the relevant monitoring period'. Residents of Marneuli Street raised grievances about vibration from operating machinery in early 2018, and the fund and contractor identified a method through which locals would no longer be exposed to noise and vibration during works. A fourth complaint, from 18 residents of Marneuli Street on 11 October 2018, concerned resettlement compensation. Of 95 visually impaired residents identified by the fund, 10 had died, 8 had moved out, 35 attended a meeting with relatives and 42 were contacted individually (ADB CRP, 2019).
cases.outcome: ADB's Compliance Review Panel found the project non-compliant in six areas and monitored a remedial action plan. At the borrower's request the scope of the Section 2 works was cut from 6.8 km to 3.5 km. By November 2019 the noise abatement package for the Ponichala stretch — a 560-metre acoustic tunnel covering both carriageways, an 880-metre wall 5 metres high and a 188-metre wall 8 metres high — had not been started, because of what the Panel was told was continued resistance from residents to the Ponichala section, and the measures to remove loose parts from buildings and secure annexes were listed as not yet implemented. Because the properties of the first three groups of complainants were not required by the project, those complainants were not among the people addressed by the land acquisition and resettlement plan (ADB CRP, 2019).

sources.title: Georgia: Sustainable Urban Transport Investment Program – Tranche 3, Compliance Review Panel Second Annual Monitoring Report
Sustainable Urban Transport Investment Program – Tranche 3: Semi-Annual Social Monitoring Report, January–June 2018

cases.confidence_note: The property acquisitions and the cutting of 57 red-list trees come from ADB's own monitoring and compliance documents, both of which I downloaded and read in full: the Compliance Review Panel's second annual monitoring report, 58 pages, and the semi-annual social monitoring report for January–June 2018, about 2,960 words. The harm the three sets of complainants asked about — noise and vibration inside their flats — was not established. The Panel's wording for building 28a is 'likely harm', its report records no confirmed physical damage to their buildings, and it says no construction activity had occurred in the areas where they live during the monitoring period. That hedge is the Panel's and is left as it stands. The 312 land plots, 29.5 hectares, 692 structures, 282 households and 33 businesses are the project's planned totals, written in the Panel's report in the future tense, and are not counts of what had happened. The 57 trees are recorded as what the Panel 'was informed'; no separate forestry record was opened. The social monitoring report's own figures are inconsistent on whether the two-storey building held 40 or 41 apartments: its narrative says 40, its account of the structural study says 41, and no source explains the gap. The demolition of the state-owned two-storey building was carried out on the residents' own written application. The first source URL keeps the double-encoded %2520 form that ADB's own site serves; the plain %20 form returns 404.

cases.title: Peshawar landfill at Ghari Faiz Ullah: 99 acres taken, open dumping and unpaid owners
cases.place: Ghari Faiz Ullah, about 19 km south of the Peshawar Ring Road, Peshawar district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
cases.point: Approximate. The ADB corrective action plan places the landfill at Ghari Faiz Ullah, about 19 km south of the Peshawar Ring Road, and gives no coordinates; the point is set in that direction from the city and is not a surveyed location.

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Loan 4160-PAK, US$380 million from ordinary capital resources, and Grant 0816-PAK, US$5 million from the Asian Development Fund, both approved 10 December 2021, signed 15 December 2021, effective 11 April 2022, closing 30 June 2028. Project 51036-002, classed A for environment and A for involuntary resettlement (ADB project page).

lenders.name: Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank
lenders.role: Loan 8412-PAK, US$200 million of co-financing, approved 16 December 2021, signed 15 December 2021, effective 11 May 2022 (ADB project page).

cases.conditions: The money funds water, sewerage, solid waste and green infrastructure in five Khyber Pakhtunkhwa cities — Abbottabad, Kohat, Mardan, Mingora and Peshawar; ADB says the project will benefit up to 3.5 million people (ADB project page). For the Peshawar landfill subproject ADB required an Implementable Corrective Action Plan, whose budget table gives a grand total of PKR 238,752,828, and the plan was prepared 'to bring the subproject in compliance with the ADB SPS requirements to enable the subproject to be considered for ADB financing' (ADB, Implementable Corrective Action Plan, April 2023).
cases.community: ADB's own corrective action plan for the Peshawar Integrated Solid Waste Management System records that the Local Government and Rural Development department acquired 792 kanal, 99 acres, in 2017 for a landfill site near village Ghari Faiz Ullah, near Shamshato refugee camp, about 19 kilometres from the Peshawar Ring Road, and that the land was handed to the Water Sewerage and Sanitation Company in 2018 and 'since then is being used as an open waste dumping site'. The land belongs to 234 displaced persons. The plan says 98 per cent of it is barren, undulated storm-water catchment, with the remaining 2 per cent under timber and fruit trees. 20.8 per cent of the acquired land came from one landowner with a total holding of 20.59 acres, only 1.5 acres of it agricultural. The document says the land acquisition and resettlement process 'did not meet the principles of ADB's Safeguard Policy Statement (SPS) 2009', naming the use of section 17/4/6, the urgency clause of the Land Acquisition Act 1894, 'which denies the people right to appeal and record their concerns', and under-assessment of land and non-land assets. One displaced person 'lost all his productive land i.e. 100% (6.25 acres)'. Two structures of mud and brick, used to house farm labour on an orange orchard, are affected, as are one tube well, 30 orange trees and 90 non-fruit trees, mostly acacia used for fuel wood. The total number of vulnerable displaced persons is 63: 43 landowners, of whom 39 fall below the poverty line on an income under PKR 20,000 a month and 4 are women-headed households, plus 20 informal waste collectors who also fall below the poverty line and depend on recyclables from the dumpsite. The Board of Revenue assessed compensation of PKR 159 million; payment started in May 2020 and 149 landowners, which the document puts at 65 per cent, had been paid PKR 120 million. 'Payments to 85 landowners of PKR 39 million is pending mainly due to inheritance mutation issues, children under age and absence of bank accounts'; a later paragraph adds disagreement with the assessed rates, meagre amounts and absentee owners, and says 29 of the 85 are women. An independent valuation study worked out a differential of 31.43 per cent on the 99 acres: PKR 157,808,199 as determined by the Land Acquisition Collector against a replacement cost of PKR 207,411,811, a gap of PKR 49,603,612. Nine consultation sessions were held with displaced persons between March 2020 and May 2021, with 48 men and women taking part, 14 of them women. Participants said that the site 'is not suitable for open dumping of waste material as it is close to population and the entire area is engulfed with very bad odor', that 'The incidence of diseases in both men and women and especially children has increased due to open/unmanaged dumping of waste', that 'The open dumping has affected the drinking water quality and the water borne diseases are on the rise', that heavy truck movement had badly affected the road surface, and that the government 'has only offered 30% less value for the land that they acquired' (ADB, Implementable Corrective Action Plan, April 2023).
cases.outcome: The corrective action plan's purpose was to bring the subproject into line with ADB's Safeguard Policy Statement so that it could be considered for ADB financing; the differential between the Board of Revenue rates and the independent valuation was to be paid by the project management unit from its own resources, and ADB's record says the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government asked the ADB mission to use part of the loan proceeds to reimburse compensation payments (ADB, Implementable Corrective Action Plan, April 2023). A separate compliance review request on the wider project, CRP 2022/5, was received on 27 December 2022; ADB's accountability mechanism page records that 'the complainants withdrew their complaint following receipt of adequate compensation' on 28 December 2022, before the Compliance Review Panel could begin processing it, so the Panel made no findings. ADB's complaint register holds 64 entries under this project name, the most recent SPF-2026-44-15-0264.

sources.title: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Cities Improvement Project: Implementable Corrective Action Plan, Peshawar Integrated Solid Waste Management System and Landfill Site
Compliance review: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Cities Improvement Project (CRP 2022/5)

cases.confidence_note: The land taking, the under-valuation, the unpaid owners and the open dumping all come from ADB's own April 2023 corrective action plan, a 137-page document ADB published under the project; I read its main body, roughly the first 30 pages, in full and searched the annexes for each figure quoted here. The link is contested on timing and ADB's own document is the reason. The 99 acres were acquired in 2017, four years before the ADB loan was approved on 10 December 2021, and the plan says plainly that 'The land was acquired by LG&RD as a part of its development plan for the city and not in anticipation of ADB's financing.' Against that, what is recorded as continuing while ADB and AIIB money was in place is the non-payment — 85 of 234 owners and PKR 39 million still pending in April 2023, sixteen months after the loan was approved — and the open dumping, which the document says has gone on since the site was handed over in 2018. ADB brought the site into its project, required the 31.43 per cent differential to be paid, and records that the provincial government asked for part of the loan proceeds to be used to reimburse the compensation. The reports of odour, rising illness and spoiled drinking water are what consultation participants told the project's own consultants; no health study was opened and no monitoring data on the drinking water was opened. ADB's own finding that the 2017 acquisition fell short of its 2009 Safeguard Policy Statement is a finding about the lender and carries nothing on its own.

cases.title: Sahiwal water and sanitation works: 196.35 acres taken for the plant, sewage standing at homes
cases.point: Sahiwal city, where the ADB-financed wastewater treatment plant site and the PICIIP-03 Lot 2 sewer works are. Neither ADB document opened gives coordinates.

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Loan 3562-PAK, US$200 million from ordinary capital resources, of a US$250 million Punjab Intermediate Cities Improvement Investment Project, project 46526-007, approved 19 September 2017 with the original closing date of 30 June 2024 extended to 30 June 2026. The remaining US$50 million came from the Government of Pakistan, which on-lent the ADB proceeds to the Government of Punjab on the same terms. ADB's project page lists cofinancing of 0.00. The Government was responsible for financing land acquisition and resettlement costs (ADB project page; ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/6).

cases.conditions: The loan funded water and sanitation works in the cities of Sahiwal and Sialkot. The project is category B for environment, A for involuntary resettlement and C for Indigenous Peoples. Contract PICIIP-03 Package Sahiwal Water and Sanitation Lot 2 was awarded in October 2020 and the completed works were handed to the Sahiwal Water and Sanitation Agency on 30 June 2026, with the contractor liable for defects until a performance certificate due 30 June 2027. ADB screened Lot 2 as category C for involuntary resettlement on the basis that the sewer works stayed inside the existing government right-of-way and needed no land acquisition or displacement. A corrective action plan was prepared and signed on site on 27 April 2026 (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/6).
cases.community: Two things happened in Sahiwal. For the wastewater treatment plant at Mouza Muhammad Pur and Chak 66-GD, ADB's own social monitoring reports record that a total of 196.35 acres of land was to be acquired, with 142 displaced persons, 271 trees, 10 irrigation tube wells and 21 building structures affected (ADB social monitoring report, 6th semiannual report, January 2023). ADB's own published account of the case says 'The complainants are composed of 18 households, who were the owners or occupiers of 40 acres of the 196.35 acres acquired by the PMU to build a wastewater treatment plant in Sahiwal.' They argued the compensation offered would not buy land of similar quality and size in the same locality, and said the replacement parcel offered was not equivalent. Their complaint form reads: 'This piece of land where we try to raise dairy animals is our only source of income. This will impact our family income and we will have no other source of livelihood. Therefore, please don't acquire our land...' ADB's Complaint Receiving Officer first received the complaint in December 2020 and forwarded it to the Office of the Special Project Facilitator in January 2021; the matter was formally brought under the problem-solving process in October 2022, and OSPF received the complaint about the project on 17 October 2022. A second complaint from two other affected households came on 30 May 2023 and the two were merged, as cases SPF-2022-16-02-0136 and SPF-2023-07-04-0146. The complainants also filed a case in the Lahore High Court. The project management unit said the compensation could not be increased and that an independent valuation study had already raised it. OSPF and the ADB project team then asked the unit to look again at how much land the plant needed. The unit found the plant could be redesigned to need about 20 acres less on the northern side of the 196-acre site. The unit applied to the Punjab Board of Revenue to denotify 20.22 acres. The Board of Revenue advised that the Land Acquisition Rules did not permit the denotification the parties had agreed, and the unit's legal team told it the Board believed all of the original owners of the denotified land, not only the complainants, must be given the chance to buy it back. The area slated for denotification was therefore cut from 20.220 acres to 15.275 acres. On 20 January 2024 the complainants and the project team signed a memorandum of understanding at a joint meeting in Lahore; the complainants accepted the compensation rate offered for the retained land and non-land assets, around 25 acres, and agreed to withdraw the Lahore High Court case once the freed land was officially denotified. At a meeting in Sahiwal on 6 and 7 May 2024, 17 of the 18 households submitted their applications for compensation vouchers and received their payments; the last was waiting on the transfer of land records to legal heirs (ADB, Taking Less Land, 2025). ADB's social monitoring report for July to December 2024 says 15.275 acres was descoped and belongs to 16 displaced persons, that all complainants of the plant received compensation payment under the signed memorandum during the reporting period, and that the Punjab Provincial Cabinet approved the denotification on 19 December 2024 at its 21st meeting; the report for January to June 2025 says the land was handed to the complainants in June 2025 for them to divide among themselves. Separately, on the Lot 2 sewer works, two residents of Sahiwal complained to ADB on 15 June 2026 that an approximately 1,800-foot sewer pipeline had been laid in what they called a zigzag alignment close to their homes, that sewage stood in front of houses for almost three months with foul odours, that trenches were left open and access blocked, that rain waterlogged the area, and that household sewer connections were lost for more than two months, with temporary 3 to 4 inch plastic pipes put in during June 2026. One wrote of 'financial business loss of shops, with sewerage water damaging to our house'. The authorities told the Compliance Review Panel a different duration: the Panel records that the Local Government department, the project unit, the city unit, the water agency and the supervision consultant 'accepted that overflowing and stagnant sewage water was occurring as described by the Complainants during the time the bypass was created and the existing sewerage pipe was being replaced by the new pipes', and that this was dewatered within 48 hours of the complaint being registered with the project's grievance mechanism. No source reconciles the two accounts of how long the sewage stood. The Panel's own finding is that 'the Complainants experienced temporary impacts during the construction phase relating to open excavated trenches (garra), obstructed access, overflowing and stagnant sewage water and foul odors resulting in elevated safety and health-related risks to the Complainants', experienced variously between April and May 2026. The complainants told the Panel that until the dewatering was done they 'faced grave inconvenience, particularly due to the foul odor and restricted access', that the effect was worst on school-going children, and that one of them had to rent a motor rickshaw from 20 April to 8 May 2026 because the roads were inundated. The Panel found all the construction-related impacts had been addressed by the time of its field visit, and the complainants confirmed that. Sand filling and household connections were completed by 22 June 2026 and the final asphalt on 20 August 2026. The Panel notes that no private land was acquired for the sewer line, as the complainants also acknowledged (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/6).
cases.suppression: The complainants also reported intimidation, threats of criminal proceedings, harassment, a shove on 15 June 2026 while one was photographing waterlogging, and an incident on 19 April 2026 in which a family was confined to its residence overnight by pooled sewage water and smoke from a burning cattle-dung heap outside. ADB Management said it had assessed the allegations separately and found no evidence that the incidents occurred. The Compliance Review Panel said it was 'not in a position to ascertain if the alleged incidents took place' and urged Management to stay mindful of retaliation risks (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/6).
cases.outcome: The 2022 land complaint ended in the 20 January 2024 memorandum of understanding, the denotification of 15.275 acres approved by the Punjab Provincial Cabinet on 19 December 2024, payment to 17 of 18 households at the May 2024 meeting, and the handover of the land in June 2025 (ADB, Taking Less Land, 2025; ADB social monitoring reports). ADB's Accountability Mechanism Annual Report 2025 describes the outcome as an 'engineering redesign of a wastewater treatment plant that avoided the acquisition of 15–20 acres of prime agricultural land'. The 2026 sewer complaint was found ineligible for compliance review on 25 September 2026: the Compliance Review Panel judged the concerns localised rather than systemic, found the harms adequately addressed with no ongoing harm, and so found the request outside paragraphs 179 and 180 of the Accountability Mechanism Policy. Ten of the project's 12 planned subprojects were completed and handed over by the loan closing date; the Sialkot wastewater treatment plant and the water metering subproject were left for the government to fund. ADB's register holds 20 entries under this project name, the most recent SPF-2026-27-07-0247.

cases.confidence_note: The land half of this case is now sourced entirely to ADB's own documents, and the Devdiscourse summary the draft rested on has been removed. ADB's 2025 problem-solving publication 'Taking Less Land' carries the 18 households, the 40 of 196.35 acres, the 20.22 to 15.275 acre reduction and its reason, the 20 January 2024 memorandum and the 17 of 18 households paid at the 6–7 May 2024 meeting; ADB's borrower-prepared social monitoring reports carry the 196.35 acres, the 142 displaced persons, the 19 December 2024 cabinet approval and the June 2025 handover. Two ADB documents give different counts for the owners of the denotified land — the publication says 18 households, the monitoring report for July to December 2024 says 16 displaced persons — and no source explains the gap; ADB's Accountability Mechanism Annual Report 2025 gives the area as '15–20 acres' rather than 15.275. Both figures are printed. The sewage standing in front of homes is not only the complainants' word for it: the Panel records that the project authorities accepted overflowing and stagnant sewage water was occurring during the bypass period, and the Panel's own finding is that the complainants experienced temporary impacts between April and May 2026. The 'almost three months' duration is the complaint's figure only; the authorities told the Panel the water was removed within 48 hours of the grievance being registered, and no source reconciles the two. 'Grave inconvenience' is what the complainants told the Panel, not a Panel finding. The Panel made no finding on the shop losses, which rest on the complaint alone. The Panel found no private land was acquired for the Lot 2 sewer, a separate matter from the plant site. The intimidation and overnight confinement are unresolved: Management says it found no evidence the incidents occurred and the Panel could not ascertain whether they did. I downloaded the Panel report and read it in full, including both annexes.

cases.title: Batumi Bypass Road: 46 hectares bought out, one house priced 20 per cent below an independent valuation
cases.point: Approximate, on the 14.3 km bypass alignment east of Batumi; ADB's report places the complainant's house near the crossing of the project road and the Batumi–Akhaltsikhe road at Interchange #4, and gives no coordinates.

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Loan 3520-GEO: Batumi Bypass Road Project, US$114.00 million from ordinary capital resources. Approved 28 March 2017, signed 12 June 2017, effective 11 October 2017, original closing date 31 December 2023 revised to 31 December 2026. ADB's project page for 50064-001 gives the loan's financing plan as a project cost of US$201.20 million with US$114.00 million from ADB and US$87.20 million counterpart. ADB's own 2020 publication calls it 'The $228 million Batumi Bypass Road Project' and 'ADB's first cofinanced project with the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank in Georgia'. AIIB's project document gives ADB's share as EUR 108.2 million. No source opened explains the differences between these figures (ADB project page 50064-001; ADB, Office of the Special Project Facilitator, Lessons Learned, 2020; AIIB project document).

lenders.name: Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank
lenders.role: Loan 8328-GEO: Batumi Bypass Road Project, US$114.00 million of cofinancing. ADB's project page gives approval 15 June 2017, signing 17 June 2017 and effectivity 12 October 2017. AIIB's own project document records USD 114.0 million committed (ADB project page 50064-001; AIIB project document).

cases.conditions: The loans fund a new two-lane bypass of about 14.3 km on the east–west highway, skirting the port city of Batumi, together with 200 km of international highways and secondary roads under performance-based maintenance contracts, a new Poti Bridge and approach roads and a new Bakurtsikhe–Tsnori road. The project was approved on 28 March 2017 and is categorised A for environment and A for involuntary resettlement (ADB, Office of the Special Project Facilitator, Lessons Learned, 2020). AIIB's document gives a total project cost of USD 315.2 million, made up of USD 114.0 million (AIIB), EUR 108.2 million (ADB) and USD 87.2 million (Government of Georgia). Land was bought out under land acquisition and resettlement plans administered by the Roads Department.
cases.community: ADB's published account of the project's land take records that, based on the detailed inventory prepared during the resettlement-plan preparation in 2016, 963 privately owned land parcels were identified as affected, that total private land to be acquired is 46 hectares, and that there are 741 affected households comprising 4,051 affected persons. Of those, the document says 369 households 'have been or will be' physically displaced and 562 households, comprising 3,024 affected persons, 'have been or will be severely affected', meaning physically displaced or losing 10 per cent or more of income-producing assets. On 2 October 2018 a household whose land and assets had been acquired for the project complained to ADB's Office of the Special Project Facilitator, alleging a GEL100,000 difference, about $40,000, between the market value and the compensation the Roads Department had paid for its property. The government's position was that the compensation was fair and based on accurate valuation and that the complainant had accepted it, so the claim was unsubstantiated. The complainant said it had signed the contract and taken the payment because a government letter indicated that if the offered price were not accepted, expropriation procedures would be initiated: 'The complainant was worried that it would lose everything and thus, reluctantly agreed to the compensation offered.' ADB's account records that documentation showed the complainant had continuously objected to the amount and had hired a different valuation entity that assessed the land much higher, and that 'Despite these objections and complaints with the local GRM, the complainant's position had been dismissed every time.' The office 'found that there was indeed a possibility of undervaluation of the complainant's property and urged the RD to reopen the case', but the Roads Department was reluctant. ADB's Central and West Asia Department then engaged Colliers International as external valuation expert under the International Valuation Standards 2017. It inspected and valued the land on 5 March 2019, with an effective valuation date of 1 November 2016 to match the project's own, and the independent valuation 'determined that the value of the property was about 20% higher than the original project valuation'. The compensation eventually paid was based on that valuation. The same document lists the other complaints the project drew: compensation rates, inclusion in the resettlement plan, property registration, damage to infrastructure or assets, a plant appraisal, and one about drinking water and a new fence (ADB, Office of the Special Project Facilitator, Lessons Learned, 2020).
cases.outcome: Several rounds of discussions facilitated by ADB's office were held between ADB and the government in May 2019, after which the Roads Department reconsidered its position, reopened the case and negotiated a settlement based on the difference between what it had originally paid and the independent valuation. The complainant signed the negotiated contract on 27 June 2019 and full payment was confirmed on 29 June 2019, which concluded the case. ADB's office recorded that the grievance mechanism was too slow and not neutral enough to catch the problem early, that complainants felt consultation was neither meaningful nor timely, and that the root cause was poorly substantiated valuations. The document does not state the final settlement amount. ADB's register holds five complaints under this project name, from SPF-2017-09-01-0066 to SPF-2026-42-01-0262.

The facility was approved 26 September 2013; Tranche 2, project 42266-025, was approved 16 August 2016, signed 21 November 2016 and became effective 10 January 2017, with an approved loan closing date of 31 August 2023. cases.conditions: The loan financed water supply, sewerage and drainage packages in Kolkata. Contract SD13, sewerage and drainage on M.G. Road, was awarded to Simplex Infrastructures Ltd on 11 November 2016; the last open-cut trunk sewer section under it was restored on 31 December 2022, and ADB Management says the unfinished remainder was paid for by the Government of West Bengal and the Kolkata Municipal Corporation. Contract WS16, water transmission, was awarded to a Furnace Fabrica India Ltd and Ramky Infrastructure Ltd joint venture on 28 March 2017; work started 19 May 2017 and finished 28 February 2023 (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/4).

cases.community: ADB Management's response to the Compliance Review Panel states that 121 project-affected persons under the SD13 sewerage and drainage package and 154 under WS16 were identified through a field verification conducted immediately before implementation, 275 in all. Management says the impacts 'principally comprised temporary disruption and income loss to roadside vendors during pipe-laying works', that livelihood assistance was initially assessed on 10 days of disruption and raised to 30 days because open-cut construction in some high-traffic sections could take longer, and that uniform assistance equal to 30 days of income loss therefore exceeded the minimum entitlement in the approved matrix. Management says the verification confirmed there was no physical displacement or permanent loss of livelihood. For SD13 the resettlement plan had estimated 24 affected persons against the 121 later verified; Management says the increase 'does not indicate any concealment or underreporting'. Management reports a three-tier grievance mechanism which received and processed 1,647 grievances across Tranche 2, including 81 under SD13 and 29 under WS16, and says the available records did not identify unresolved project-related grievances under those two packages. Six vendors from Kolkata, represented by Growthwatch India and asking for confidentiality, complained to the Compliance Review Panel on 13 June 2026, attaching a list of about 124 other project-affected persons who said they had been similarly affected. They said they had operated shops in the area for about 25 to 30 years, that their shops were dismantled in 2019 at their own cost, and that 'we were prohibited from returning to our sites of operation and some of us even detained, when attempting to' re-establish their businesses. They said they had been reduced to vending from 'hand-held tea or other carts' or to daily wage activities, that some had moved away, and that they received INR 15,000 each on 18 August 2019 as compensation for about one month of temporary income loss, which they considered inadequate because the loss ran well beyond a month and included the cost of dismantling and of setting up alternative structures: 'We are still waiting to have our previous shops back, and with them, our former earnings.' Management says the opposite on the central point — 'ADB staff found no records showing that the Project required the permanent demolition of roadside shops' — and that neither the resettlement plans nor the verification found physical displacement from housing. In 2019 ADB reviewed concerns about four roadside shopkeepers raised by the Indian Social Action Forum through the NGO Forum on ADB, and says it confirmed they had been identified as project-affected persons, that their business structures remained intact and that livelihood assistance had been paid. Management attributes what happened after 2023 to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation's own road widening, which began on 17 February 2023 and which it says ADB neither financed nor supervised (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/4).
cases.suppression: The complainants say some of them were detained when they tried to re-establish their businesses, and that they faced intimidation when they raised complaints. ADB Management ties the alleged intimidation to the period after 2023 and to the municipal road-widening rather than to the ADB-financed works. The Compliance Review Panel made no finding either way (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/4).
cases.outcome: In its Report on Eligibility dated 2 September 2026 the Compliance Review Panel determined the complaint ineligible under paragraph 142(iv) of the 2012 Accountability Mechanism Policy, which excludes complaints about a project for which two or more years have passed since the loan closing date. It found that 31 August 2023 was the formally approved loan closing date, set by a memorandum of 20 October 2022 and never further extended, so the two-year period expired on 31 August 2025, before the complaint was filed on 13 June 2026. The 14 June 2024 date on ADB's Project Data Sheet was the financial closing of the loan account, not the loan closing date. The Panel found the data sheet's milestones table 'not self-explanatory' and said ADB Management's 6 March 2026 email to the complainants' representative did not identify the governing date either, and that the representative 'could reasonably have understood 14 June 2024 to be the relevant date'; but it held this had not prejudiced them because the period calculated from 31 August 2023 had already expired before they made their inquiry in January 2026. It said paragraph 142(iv) left it no discretion to substitute the financial closing date. The Panel wrote that its determination 'should not be understood as a finding on ADB's compliance or noncompliance with the applicable safeguard policies and procedures, the alleged harms, or the causal relationship between the alleged harms and the ADB-financed project.'

cases.title: Malolos–Clark Railway: tagged in 2018, still waiting, and a 2026 complaint of demolition without compensation
cases.place: San Fernando and Angeles, Pampanga, along the Malolos–Clark railway right-of-way, Philippines
cases.point: Approximate, at Barangay Maimpis, San Fernando City, Pampanga, one of the places along the right-of-way named in VERA Files' reporting.

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: US$2.75 billion for civil works — viaducts, stations, tunnels and depot buildings. The first tranche of US$1.3 billion, P66.83 billion at the 11 July 2019 exchange rate, was signed on 11 July 2019; its validity was extended from 21 December 2021 to 21 December 2022 and then to 30 June 2024. ADB had disbursed P47.40 billion by December 2023 (VERA Files). ADB project 52083-001 (ADB Accountability Mechanism).

lenders.role: US$2 billion for tracks, electrification, signalling, telecommunications, rolling stock and consulting services (VERA Files).

cases.conditions: The loans fund the 53 km Malolos–Clark section of the North–South Commuter Railway. JICA recommended a consistent 30-metre right-of-way where the legacy Philippine National Railways corridor is about 10 to 20 metres wide, so more land had to be bought, most of it in dense residential areas. The Philippine government paid P74.67 million in commitment fees on undrawn loans in 2022 alone, at 0.15 per cent a year on undrawn amounts, which VERA Files attributes to the delays. An ADB cost–benefit analysis put the economic internal rate of return at 12.3 per cent and said the project 'remains viable in all cases' in the scenarios it tested, including a two-year delay (VERA Files).

companies.name: Italian-Thai Development Public Company Limited
companies.role: Civil works contractor on contract package N-03, covering parts of Angeles and San Fernando; a city engineer told VERA Files its slow progress rate was because of a lack of right-of-way, with only about 30 per cent of the area in Angeles workable

cases.community: Rosa Lebosana, 41, of Barangay Maimpis in San Fernando City, has lived since 2003 in a 50-square-metre house with her husband and three children. Her house was surveyed and tagged on 9 November 2018 and sits partly inside the 30-metre right-of-way. Six years after the tagging she said the Department of Transportation had not followed through and local leaders could not answer her questions; her family had still not moved. Her relocation option is Barangay Panipuan, about 9.7 km away, where relocated families take a housing loan from the National Housing Authority and get a land title from the local government. JICA's 2018 census recorded 1,416 potentially affected households; National Housing Authority data for 2024 showed the number of affected informal settler families had risen by about 108.70 per cent. As of September 2024 fewer than 5 per cent of affected informal settler families had been verified and resettled, and in Pampanga 112 of 1,936 had been relocated. By October 2024 the Department of Transportation had acquired 31 parcels, 4.9 hectares, of the estimated 45.5 hectares needed. In San Fernando, 67 row houses in Barangay Calulut had been built and occupied and 312 units in Barangay Panipuan were ready for occupancy by October 2024, while a planned 280-unit site in Panipuan had not started because the land has to be reclassified out of a Strategic Agriculture and Fisheries Development Zone. Demolition of houses along the main line cannot go ahead until replacement housing is ready: without those prerequisites, VERA Files reports, 'the demolition of houses along the main railway line cannot proceed.' On 7 October 2026 a complaint was filed with ADB's accountability mechanism against the project, SPF-2026-43-04-0263, with the issue recorded as 'House demolition without compensation' (ADB Accountability Mechanism).
cases.outcome: Construction in San Fernando was 28.97 per cent complete as of August 2024, and the 53 km section's completion moved from 2024 to 2028; San Fernando's own projected completion moved from 2027 to 2028 and then to 2029. VERA Files traces the delay to the 2018–19 parcellary plans, which contained errors found when work resumed in 2022 and had to be revalidated; the National Economic and Development Authority's August 2024 portfolio review blamed 'prolonged review and approval' of parcellary plans that 'did not meet set standards'. Contract Package No. 03, covering portions of Angeles and San Fernando, suffers the brunt of the problem; a city engineer said the slow progress of its contractor, Italian-Thai Development, was because of a lack of right-of-way, with the workable areas in Angeles for package N-03 at only about 30 per cent of the supposed 100 per cent. The transport department's right-of-way team had four members at the start and 48 by October 2024, against a target of 137. Its planning undersecretary called the lack of on-ground staff the real root cause and said 'Just imagine the burden if you are one person handling 200 parcels.' Angeles City's planning office said the department had not given it parcellary maps showing affected areas and structures, which made issuing building permits near the railway harder. ADB's register holds five complaints under the Malolos–Clark and South Commuter railway project names between 2025 and 2026.

Fails tests 2 and 3: no construction, so no harm. A 2024 NGO report filed to the Council of Europe (rm.coe.int, the Svaneti/Nenskra complainants' report, which I read in full at about 1,400 words) records that local people say work has not started on Nenskra and that no construction company had been selected, with the government saying it expected works to resume 'by the end of the year, 2024 at the latest'. OC Media (2020) records that construction has been on hold since Salini Impregilo left in October 2018, and that Bankwatch's field investigation found over 200 people 'would lose' homes, land or pastures — future loss. Bankwatch's own September 2017 blog says pasture and wooden cabins 'would be temporarily or permanently lost' and records no confirmed loss. The EBRD and EIB complaint mechanisms found the project non-compliant with their standards on land acquisition, resettlement, economic displacement, Indigenous issues, cultural heritage, disclosure and engagement, but those are findings about the banks, not records of harm, and neither bank had signed its loan agreement (EBRD $214 million, EIB $150 million, both approved). ADB is listed only as a prospective investor. One item I could not open: business-humanrights.org's summary of a later NGO report saying JSC Nenskra Hydro failed to provide adequate compensation for people affected — both the English and French URLs returned a client error from the site and nothing of either page was retrieved, so whether land was in fact acquired is unresolved and someone should retry that page.

CHECKER: drop confirmed, and the open question closed. The business-humanrights.org page the writer could not open does open: fetched with an ordinary browser user-agent it returns HTTP 200, not a client error. It is dated 10 October 2017, not later, and it is only a pointer to the same Bankwatch report plus a company response from JSC Nenskra Hydro. I then downloaded and read in full the underlying report itself, Bankwatch's 'Failing local communities: Report on the Land Assessment and Livelihoods Restoration Plan for the Nenskra Hydropower Project', September 2017, 9,138 words. Every loss in it is prospective: households 'would lose' compensation, 'will lose' access and income, and the pastures and cabins are described as being inside the 'land take area'. It records no completed acquisition and no completed loss. Nothing is left to retry on this lead.

dropped.candidate: Georgian Railway Green Bond (Zestaponi–Kharagauli–Khashuri landslides), CRP 2025/9
dropped.reason:
Fails the link test, on the office's own words. The harm is real and documented: Democracy and Freedom Watch reports a roughly three-kilometre rupture across the mountainside at Khemaghali and Ghverki in Kharagauli municipality, first noticed as cracks on 26 May 2025, with about 107 households in the two villages before the slide, most told to leave and rent elsewhere, most homes in Khemaghali abandoned with cracked walls, government rent support of up to 500 lari a month and many villagers left off the registries. But the Compliance Review Panel found the complaint outside the scope of compliance review because the alleged harms were not related to ADB-financed components, stating that 'The construction of the tunnels falls strictly outside the activities financed by ADB' — ADB's $20 million in Georgian Railway green bonds since 2021 went to substation renovation, bridges, culverts, track laying, electrification and water works, not tunnelling (Sakartvelos Ambebi, reporting the Panel's decision). Residents say experts privately linked the slide to blasting for railway construction in 2019–2022; no official geological finding on the cause has been published. If a future document ties the blasting to an ADB-financed component, this becomes a case.

CHECKER: drop confirmed, and the Panel's reasoning now comes from ADB rather than from press reporting of it. ADB's Accountability Mechanism Annual Report 2025 states: 'Following initial assessment and review of project documentation, the CRP determined that the complaint was not admissible. The CRP found that ADB financing had not been used for new railway lines or tunnel-related works, and that the alleged impacts related to activities outside the scope of ADB financing.' ADB's complaint register gives the complaint as 2025-118, received 17 October 2025, project 55132-001, forwarded to the CRP on 7 November 2025. The link test fails on the office's own words.

Specialists hired by ADB's office found the chosen alignment 'the least harmful and within the policy framework' against ADB's 2009 Safeguard Policy Statement, Indian courts upheld the decision and an appeal was dismissed, and a February 2024 memorandum with eight of the sixteen households provided temporary relocation support, a baseline structural stability survey funded by ADB's office and a commitment to repair verified damage, with pre-construction surveys done for 14 of the 16 apartments by June 2024. Measures to catch damage if it happens are not damage. The ADB publication 'A Rail Too Far?' (June 2025, 16 pages) would be the place to check: its landing page served only metadata, abstract and contents, and the PDF itself was not opened. If its text records damage found by those surveys, this becomes a case.
